name: Pangasinan
notes: Pangasinan (Salitan Pangasinan), Northern Luzon (Malayo-Polynesian) language of the Philippines. Latin orthography: the 26 basic Latin letters plus the digraph ⟨ng⟩ /ŋ/. Native vocabulary has /a i ɨ u/ plus /ɛ ɔ/ largely in loans; the close central /ɨ/ is written ⟨e⟩ in the traditional spelling and ⟨ë⟩ in the revised one, so ⟨e⟩ carries both candidates. /tʃ dʒ ʃ/ occur chiefly in Spanish and English loans.

sources.author: Benton, Richard A.
sources.title: Pangasinan Reference Grammar (PALI Language Texts: Philippines)
sources.publisher: University of Hawaii Press (open access edition, CC BY-NC-SA, ScholarSpace)
sources.notes: Phonology chapter, read in the vowel, consonant-chart and orthography sections. p. 3: four vowel phonemes /a e i o/ for all speakers, a fifth /E/ for many (both /e/ and /E/ written ⟨e⟩), and ⟨o u⟩ standing for one phoneme /o/ for most speakers. pp. 14-15: thirteen consonant phonemes /b d g p t k m n ŋ r s h l/ plus /y w/, with /ch/ (also /ts/) the one marginal phoneme worth noting. pp. 35-37: /E/ written ⟨e⟩, /o/ written ⟨o⟩ or ⟨u⟩ at random, /h/ spelled ⟨h⟩ or ⟨j⟩ (and ⟨g⟩ before e/i in Spanish words), ⟨ll⟩ = /ly/, ⟨ñ⟩ = /ny/, ⟨ng⟩ or ⟨ñg⟩ = /ŋ/, ⟨f v⟩ read as /p b/, ⟨c z⟩ as /s/. Against this map: ⟨j⟩ is /h/ in Benton's account, not dʒ; there is no /ʃ/ phoneme and no glottal-stop phoneme in his inventory, so the ⟨sh⟩ and ⟨'⟩ keys have no support there; and ⟨o u⟩ are one phoneme, not the o/ɔ versus u the map emits. Recorded here; the grapheme data is not changed in this citation.

ancestors.notes: Malayo-Polynesian, the Austronesian branch containing every Austronesian language outside Formosa.
